data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction is best drawn through the safety-vs-liveness lens from distributed systems theory: a safety property asserts that 'something bad never happens' (no incorrect state is reached), while idempotency is a specific structural guarantee about operation semantics (f(f(x))=f(x)). An append-only log requires the safety property: bad states (corrupted replay) never arise from duplicate appends. It does not require idempotency because the 'bad thing'\u2014duplicate entries\u2014is not itself a correctness violation if the replay engine filters them.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the replay engine does not filter duplicates, the finite prefix with duplicate entries violates the safety property and the system is unsafe.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the formal definition of safety used in the referenced published literature differs from the Lamport-style safety/liveness distinction, this framing may not align with the cited sources.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If duplicate entries cause downstream effects that compound (e.g., counter increment), the safety property is violated even with detection, because the damage occurs before filtering.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Safety properties in distributed systems are those that can be violated by a finite prefix (a bad thing has happened), whereas liveness properties require infinite behavior. Duplicate appends produce a finite prefix with extra entries; whether this violates safety depends on whether the replayed state is incorrect. If the replay engine treats duplicate-keyed entries as redundant, the safety property holds despite non-idempotent appends. The log needs writers that preserve the safety property (no corrupted replay), not writers whose primitive operation is idempotent.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
